content: 1. A 2012 literature review-based decision model found that a full course of antenatal corticosteroids was cost-effective at 34, 35, and 36 weeks of gestation, using a threshold of $100,000 per quality-adjusted life year (QALY). However, a partial course of antenatal corticosteroids was not cost-effective. 2. A 2019 study concluded that betamethasone reduced the total mean costs for each woman-infant pair when compared to placebo. 3. In contrast, a 2020 study, using the same data, reported that betamethasone was not cost-effective in the short term. This discrepancy was attributed to differences in cost calculations: the 2019 study only considered the primary trial outcome (neonatal respiratory morbidity within the first 72 hours), while the 2020 study included additional outcomes such as neonatal hypoglycemia (which was increased with betamethasone) and derived utilities for each outcome to calculate QALYs. 4. The 2020 study reported that late preterm antenatal corticosteroid use was slightly more expensive and generated fewer QALYs compared to placebo. 5. Antenatal corticosteroids are relatively inexpensive, easy to administer, and widely available in at least one preparation across various healthcare settings. 6. Incorporating antenatal corticosteroid therapy into existing health systems and protocols for managing women at imminent risk of preterm birth is feasible and can be achieved with minimal cost. 7. Dexamethasone sodium phosphate (4 mg/mL) is included in the WHO Essential Medicines List, but injectable betamethasone preparations are not listed. 8. Identifying women at risk of preterm birth requires skilled healthcare personnel capable of diagnosing preterm labor, excluding contraindications (e.g., maternal infection), prescribing and administering intramuscular (IM) antenatal corticosteroids, and monitoring maternal care. 9. Accurate estimation of gestational age necessitates personnel trained in obstetric ultrasound. 10. Preterm infants may require additional specialized care, including respiratory support, feeding assistance, thermoregulation, infection control, and neonatal intensive care. 11. Training healthcare personnel to administer injections, monitor neonatal side effects, and manage complications is part of standard maternity staff training. Additional training may be necessary in settings where antenatal corticosteroids are newly introduced. 12. Administering a single IM dose of antenatal corticosteroids takes approximately two minutes, but consultation time with women to discuss risks and benefits is also required. 13. Maintaining a consistent stock of antenatal corticosteroids in maternity wards and emergency departments is critical to ensuring timely treatment for women in preterm labor. 14. Some healthcare providers expressed uncertainties and lacked confidence in prescribing and administering antenatal corticosteroids in specific clinical scenarios, such as repeat dosing or use in women with diabetes, hypertension, fetal complications, infection, or premature rupture of membranes. 15. Providers also raised concerns about the research evidence supporting antenatal corticosteroid therapy, citing fears of side effects and birth defects, which may act as barriers to its use. 16. The unpredictability of preterm birth, including challenges in diagnosing imminent versus threatened preterm labor, can lead to hesitation among healthcare providers in administering antenatal corticosteroids, potentially affecting fetal exposure duration. 17. In some countries, antenatal corticosteroids are only administered at tertiary facilities with comprehensive emergency obstetric and neonatal care services. Pre-referral first-dose administration at lower-level facilities is limited due to challenges in identifying preterm labor, lack of knowledge about pre-referral dosing, and transportation issues. 18. Time constraints, high workloads, and competing tasks were identified as significant barriers to the administration of antenatal corticosteroids, particularly in the context of imminent preterm birth. 19. Evidence from trials demonstrates that antenatal corticosteroid use is effective, provided that a minimum level of maternal and preterm newborn care is available. 20. It is essential to ensure that antenatal corticosteroids are administered only to eligible women in settings where adequate maternal and preterm newborn care are available. 21. A 2020 systematic review identified issues with the quality of dexamethasone, with some samples failing due to inadequate active pharmacological ingredients, particularly in public sector and point-of-care settings. 22. The balance of effects for antenatal corticosteroid therapy varies depending on gestational age, with more favorable outcomes observed at ≤35 weeks compared to ≥34 weeks. 23. The certainty of evidence regarding maternal and neonatal outcomes is generally low to moderate, with variability in findings across different gestational ages and study designs. 24. Healthcare providers and policymakers identified insufficient budgets as a barrier to optimal procurement and distribution of antenatal corticosteroids. 25. Positive attitudes, improved knowledge, and exposure to training, conferences, guidelines, and research articles were facilitators of appropriate antenatal corticosteroid use. Conversely, outdated knowledge and gaps between research evidence and clinical experience were barriers. 26. Ensuring antenatal corticosteroids are administered in appropriate contexts with adequate maternal and neonatal care is critical to optimizing their benefits and minimizing risks.
